Gowzican: 
We are so excited to have you here. My name is Gowzican. I am 
speaking on behalf of the CBS Investment Club at Copenhagen 
Business School. The CBS Investment Club is a club run by students. 
It is an investment fund focused on Nordic equities—gathering 
students from across the university interested in the markets and 
capital allocation. For those of you who do not know Mohnish, he is 
the founder and managing partner of Pabrai Investment Funds. He is 
also the CEO of Dhandho Funds and the author of The Dhandho 
Investor. Moreover, he has some philanthropic activities. He is the 
chairman and founder of the Dakshana Foundation, where he gives 
impoverished children in India opportunities to study at IIT, which is 
equivalent to MIT in the US. Mohnish, let us go straight to the Q&A 
session. 
 
My first question for you is: What advice do you have for students 
who want to go into the investment management business and try 
to emulate maybe what Buffett has done? 
 
Mohnish: 
The first thing I would suggest is that you need to have solid evidence 
that you are a good investor and that you are likely to be a good 
steward for other people's hard-earned money.  
 
The best way to accomplish that is to have an auditable track record 
that you have built over a few years with your own funds. What I 
would recommend is to have a brokerage account that is dedicated, 
where you are not writing checks here and there, but where, later at 
some point, that account can be handed over to an audit firm and 
they can relatively easily come up with an audited record of what the 
returns have been. The first thing is that there should be some 
reasonable period of time (5, 10 years or something) where you have 
built a record and you convinced yourself that you are good at this, 
and then after that if that goes well, you go on to convince folks to 
give you money to manage. On that front, you put your energies 
behind friends, family, and fools—and the most important are the 
fools. 
 
Gowzican: 
Interesting. My next question for you is: How do you deal with 
management when researching a company? They are often good at 
sales and charismatic people. How do you manage that? 
 
Pg. 2 of 14 
Mohnish: 
You can understand the nature of management by looking at the 
historical track record. This track record is public. If that team and 
CEO have been in that position for a while, then you have some 
pretty solid data points of what they have done in the past, and that 
should give you a good indicator of what is going on. You can also 
talk to competitors to see what they think about the company and 
the individuals. You can get a good feel for all of that. You do not 
necessarily need to be interacting with management to get a view. 
In fact, interacting with management might create distortions, 
whereas you might get a cleaner view from looking at the history and 
track record. 
 
Gowzican: 
Interesting. My next question is: You have a big part of your US 
portfolio in Micron, if I remember correctly. What did you learn from 
selling Micron early? 
 
Mohnish: 
That was the investment I had made with Li Lu, who manages some 
money for Charlie Munger. Li Lu and I discussed it with Charlie. The 
investment was made around 2017, and we exited in 2023. I do not 
have any regrets about the exit because it made sense with the data 
we were seeing. Of course, it has gone up a lot since then.  
 
But the premise of the Micron investment was that there was a 
rational oligopoly of three players, SK Hynix, Micron, and Samsung, 
that controlled the memory market. The barriers to entry are 
extremely high for a fourth player to get scale in the memory 
business. There are a lot of patents, processes, capital, and different 
impediments to a fourth player having any chance of making it. We 
had a market with three players, and from what we could tell, the 
three players were acting rationally in the sense that they were all 
profitable, making money, and they were not trying to beat each 
other up.  
 
One of the things I had discussed with Charlie is whether these 
oligopoly situations were stable in terms of cash flows and business 
prospects or whether there were issues to be concerned about. 
Charlie said that Warren Buffett had studied a large number of Coke 
and Pepsi bottlers in various U.S. cities and countries around the 
world. That is an oligopoly situation with two players. He said that in 
probably 95 or 97% of markets, the Coke and Pepsi bottlers in a 
particular geography acted rationally, and both bottlers made 
money. But he said there were 3 to 5% of markets where one of the 
players decided that they wanted to increase market share. They 
became more aggressive with promotions and pricing. Of course, 
the second player has to respond to that. Even though there is brand 
loyalty, if I go to pick up a 12-pack of Coke and the 12-pack of Pepsi 
is 30% cheaper, I would switch. There is brand loyalty, but it is not 
extreme brand loyalty. In these markets where these players were 
trying to take more market share from the other player, nobody 
made any money because it was a race to the bottom. The other 
person also reacted, and then pricing went down and got more 
aggressive. You end up with markets where normally having a Coke 
Pg. 3 of 14 
bottler is a license to print money, but you would end up with 
markets in 3 to 5% of cases where nobody made money.  
 
In the Micron oligopoly situation, it was similar: these three players, 
from what we could tell in 2017—and I met with all three players, 
made several trips to Seoul, met with Hynix and Samsung, and also 
met with the senior management at Micron—understood all that, and 
they were not going to be acting irrationally.  
 
But then in 2023, there was a change when Samsung had half the 
market, 50%, and the other two players had approximately 25% each, 
and Samsung decided that they wanted greater market share. They 
got more aggressive with pricing to take more market share. Of 
course, the other two players, SK Hynix and Micron, had to react and 
respond. 
 
What happened in 2023 is that all three players lost money, and what 
was a rational market suddenly became an irrational, unpredictable 
market. By then, the stock we had bought had approximately 
doubled. It was not a great return, but it was kind of a low-teens 
annualized return from when we had bought, and the future was 
murky. We could not tell, and we were looking at negative cash 
flows. I decided to exit. Li Lu exited around the same time. Then, of 
course, two or three years later, we had the AI boom, and things 
went the other way, where now it does not matter whether the 
players are rational or not. They are not able to keep up with demand. 
They are all trying to produce full-out with the AI.  
 
It is the way it is. The investing business is an extremely forgiving 
business. One can and will be wrong the majority of the time. And 
even if one is wrong, the majority of the time, the results may be 
more than acceptable if you are following some rules.  
 
Let me give you an example. In the late '60s and early 1970s in the 
U.S., there was a concept known as the Nifty 50. The Nifty 50 was an 
approach to investing where the idea was that you bought equal 
amounts invested in the 50 strongest, most blue-chip companies in 
the U.S. You would take a portfolio and put 2% of the portfolio into 
American Express, 2% in Coca-Cola, Pepsi, GE, Kodak, Boeing, 
McDonald's, Polaroid, and so on. You would not care about the 
valuations, not care about anything; hold these great businesses, and 
the end result would be good. What ended up happening is that in 
1973 and ‘74, these companies got bid up to spectacular levels, like 
50, 60 times trailing earnings. They got expensive. In '73 and '74, 
there was a stock market crash in slow motion where over two years 
the U.S. stock market went down more than 50%, and the Nifty 50 
went down a lot more than that. It got taken out back and shot. The 
Nifty 50 was probably down like 60, 70%, and by 1975 no one had any 
interest in the Nifty 50. Everyone had sold the Nifty 50 position they 
had at steep losses.  
 
There is some controversy over whether Walmart was part of the 
Nifty 50 or not. But to help me make my point, let us make the 
Pg. 4 of 14 
assumption that Walmart was part of the Nifty 50 and that one had 
put 2% of the portfolio into Walmart. Let us assume that the people 
who invested in the Nifty 50 did not touch it or sell it in the '73, '74 
downturn or from then until now. They kept the whole thing and did 
not make any trades. Let us also make an extreme assumption that 
every holding in that Nifty 50 went to zero except Walmart. You 
made an investment in a portfolio of 50 stocks. 49 stocks have gone 
to zero, and only one stock that you bought, which is Walmart, does 
what it did. If you looked at the returns from 1972, when Walmart 
went public, to 2026 (54 years), including reinvested dividends, 
Walmart has delivered about 15 or 16% a year annualized, and the S&P 
500, 15 or 16% a year. Starting with 2%, what I am saying is that with 
that 98% going to zero and the S&P having the entire 100 cents, the 
Nifty 50 portfolio with a 98% error rate blew out the S&P by about 5% 
a year, with 49 out of 50 stocks going to zero. 
 
Now, of course, 49 out of 50 stocks did not go to zero. We still have 
McDonald's, AMEX, Coke, and a lot of the other businesses. But many 
of the stocks did go to zero, like Xerox, Kodak, Polaroid, and Digital 
Equipment. But it did not matter. The bottom line was that one 
holding was enough to offset all the other losses. If we study stock 
markets for a long period of time, let us say over the last 100 years, 
for example, the US markets, what we find is that all the returns of 
the equity markets have come from 4% of the stocks. The remaining 
96% of the stocks have done nothing. They have gone to zero or done 
nothing. All the returns (that 9, 10, 11% a year that we get) have come 
from 4% of the equities. The important thing was not to buy Walmart. 
The important thing was not to touch Walmart, to never sell it, no 
matter what was happening, no matter what the company said and 
what they reported. You kept it.  
 
The Walton family owned 46% of Walmart when it went public in 
1972. After 54 years, they own more than 46% of Walmart. The Walton 
family has never sold Walmart in 54 years. Because Walmart has 
bought back shares, they own a higher percentage of the company. 
They followed that principle of holding, but no institutional investors 
held Walmart for 54 years.  
 
The important thing with investing is what Charlie Munger said is, in 
a lifetime, we are going to get a few trips to the pie counter. When 
we get a trip to the pie counter, we have to load up on a lot of pie 
and then try not to drop that pie till you get back to your table. 
Someone asked him once, “How can one be good at selling?” His 
response was, “Do not worry about becoming good at selling. Worry 
about becoming good at finding Costco's.”  
 
We can be useless at selling. We can sell nothing. We can have a high 
error rate, as long as we recognize that something in our portfolio is 
truly exceptional. It could be a small part of the portfolio like Walmart 
at 2%. But when we find ourselves in the lucky situation of partial 
ownership of a great business, do not sell that business because it 
looks fully priced. Do not sell that business when it looks overpriced. 
Pg. 5 of 14 
If that business possibly gets egregiously overpriced, one could think 
about selling it.  
 
In 2018, I had noticed that the Turkish stock market was screening 
ultra-cheap. In fact, the cheapest in the world. I do not know 
anything about Turkey, like I know nothing about Copenhagen. But I 
have a good friend in Istanbul, who is now the second-largest equity 
fund manager in Turkey. He is a Ben Graham disciple. I told him, “I 
would love to visit Turkey, and I would love to visit the companies in 
your portfolio. Would you be open to that?” He said, “Oh, this would 
be a lot of fun, Mohnish. It would be great.” I made a trip to Turkey 
with nothing in mind other than trying to learn a bit more about this 
alien market and alien place. He sent me a list of companies that we 
were going to visit, and I never looked at the companies or studied 
them. I said that I would look at the businesses after I had met with 
them. If I met with the company and I saw something that looked 
interesting, then I would start doing research on them. What I was 
doing was that when we were driving to the business, I would start 
asking my friend questions about the business. I did not appear total 
village idiot at the meeting. I at least knew something about the 
business.  
 
The second year I visited Turkey in 2019, we were driving to this 
company, and I started asking my friend questions about it. He said, 
“The market cap is $15 million, and the liquidation value is $800 
million.” I asked him if this was a fraud. He said, “No, it is not a fraud. 
It is a simple, basic company. They rent warehouses, and I own the 
business. I have a stake in the business.” I asked him why it was so 
cheap. He said, “Well, everything in Turkey is cheap.” I had visited 
companies with him where the P/E was 0.1 (not a P/E of one; P/E of 
0.1). The company is trading at 1 month’s earnings. I had seen extreme 
stuff in Turkey.  
 
When he told me everything in Turkey is cheap, I shrugged. He is 
right. Everything in Turkey is cheap because no one is interested. 
Currency is unstable; inflation is out of control, all of this stuff.  
 
I met the company's founders, the father and son who run it. They 
seem like smart business people. I visited the warehouses that 
afternoon. They looked spectacular. They were prime. Things were 
exactly like he was saying. He said you could go to any commercial 
real estate broker in Istanbul, show them the portfolio, and they 
would tell you the portfolio is worth a billion dollars. There is $200 
million of debt, so it is worth $800 million. The market cap is like $15 
million. I was concerned because I was managing about $600 or 
$700 million. How much stock can I get? It is such a small company. 
But Turkey is a market of gamblers with high trading volumes. 
Everyone buys stocks at 10 o'clock, and they sell at 3 o'clock, and they 
want to make 10%. That is their business model. Buy at 10 o'clock, sell 
at 3 o'clock, make 10%. Good luck with that.  
 
Buffett has a quote that the stock market is a mechanism to transfer 
wealth from the active to the inactive.  
Pg. 6 of 14 
 
When I started buying the Reysas shares, I saw that the volumes 
were extremely high. The average public company in Turkey cycles 
through its float every 17 days, with high trading volumes because it 
is all gamblers and day traders. For $8 million, I got 1/3 of the 
company. I bought some more, and now we have a little over 41% of 
the company. The market cap of the company now is $1.8 billion 
dollars. The $15 million market cap in 2019 is a $1.8 billion market cap 
in 2026. The Turkish lira, which was 5 liras to the dollar in 2019 when 
I was buying, is more than 48 liras to the dollar. The lira has collapsed. 
It has gone down by more than 90%. But in dollars, we have more 
than a 120x return in 7 years. 
 
What I did not realize when I was buying the business is that my plan 
was okay; it is worth $800 million. When it gets to $600 or $700 
million or something, we will sell it. From $15 million to $600 million 
is a pretty nice ride. I was fully aware that Turkey has high inflation 
and an unstable currency being devalued a lot. But I remembered 
this story. Someone had told me once about the Coca-Cola 
company. Someone said that, let us say there is a global 
thermonuclear event. All the nukes owned by all the countries in the 
world are set off. Out of 8 billion humans, 99% are dead and gone. 
We have $80 million humans left. Everything is decimated. Someone 
somewhere creates a Coke bottling plant to start producing Coke for 
his fellow $80 million citizens. There is no currency. But people 
would be willing to trade 15 minutes of their labor for an 8-ounce 
serving of Coke. It does not matter if the currency is seashells or lira 
or dollars or cigarettes. There will be a trade available for one 
cigarette for a Coke or something like that. The Coke business would 
come back to serve the $80 million. Regardless of the currency, they 
had figured out the currencies.  
 
When I looked at the Turkish warehouse business, I thought, “What 
is a warehouse? A warehouse is land, cement, steel, concrete, and 
some paint. That is what a warehouse is.” Every one of those things 
is inflation-indexed automatically. They can do whatever they want 
to the lira. The land will cost more lira, and the paint is going to cost 
more lira. It is going to naturally move because that is the way the 
world is. It is going to move with the lira. To me, when I am buying a 
prime warehouse in a prime city of the world like Istanbul, it is 
automatically inflation-indexed, whatever their rents were. I did not 
have any concern. I specifically looked at businesses in Turkey where 
the currency and inflation are irrelevant. I said, “Bring it on. Bring on 
1000% a year of inflation. I am ready. Bring it on. You bring on 
whatever inflation you want, because I have hard assets that will 
react and adjust accordingly.” I made the bet. What I did not realize 
when I made the bet is that the father and son who ran this business 
were exceptional capital allocators. They do not invest capital if they 
do not see a return in dollars or euros and that all their money comes 
back in 2 or 3 years. They have a simple way of thinking about things. 
If the return on investment is not more than 25 to 35% a year in dollars 
or euros, they are not interested. A business that was worth $800 
million in 2019 is now worth $3 billion. Again, I can do the same math. 
Pg. 7 of 14 
I go to a broker in Istanbul and show the portfolio. They are going to 
say, “This portfolio is worth like $3.4 billion, and there is $400 million 
of debt.” The market cap is $1.8 billion. The liquidation value is $3 
billion. That $3 billion liquidation value is compounding at, let us say, 
15 to 30% a year.  
 
We had a trip to the pie counter, the first one being Micron. On the 
way back, the pie got dropped on the floor, and it was no longer 
edible. We were only able to get a double return on the money, and 
the rest of the pie was swept up in the garbage. But then there was 
a second trip to the pie counter. What am I supposed to do with 
Reysas in Turkey? What I should do is spend all my time talking to the 
students at the Copenhagen Business School and leave the Reysas 
position alone. Like Charlie says, “Do not interrupt compounding 
unnecessarily.” Now I manage a little more than $1.4 billion. The 
Reysas position is $500-$550 million.  
 
There are a few other irons in the fire that I do not think are going to 
zero. My main job description is to not do any trades. It is to sit there 
and watch the pie. Next month, I am going to Istanbul. I go to 
Istanbul once a year in September or October and meet with the 
founders of Reysas. They own 44% of the company. My investors and 
I own 41% of the company. I tell them, “This is our family business. 
Your family and my family. I know we did not start as business 
partners. I know that you are the founder, and we have subsequently 
bought in. We do not want any board seats. I do not need to tell you 
anything because anything I tell you about how to run the business 
would make the business worse. Because I am so stupid at 
everything and you are so good at everything.”  
 
We go eat blue fish at a Michelin-starred restaurant overlooking the 
Bosphorus. It is a nice dinner. I pat them on the back, and I say, “Keep 
doing what you are doing, and I will see you next year.” That is my job 
description. We are done. I hope they stay in the saddle, and I hope 
they run that business for 20, 30, 40 years or more. Recently, I have 
noticed that the son has been bringing his 11-year-old son to various 
business meetings. I said, “Amen.” Let us get the next generation 
ready so that after 40 years, the compounding can continue.  
 
Gowzican: 
Interesting, Mohnish. We have a question from Will Hansen, who is 
also a member of the Investment Club. His question is: One of your 
most recent investments is Kaspi in Kazakhstan, which appears to be 
an exceptional business. With a strong management team, high 
growth, excellent margins, and a monopoly-like competitive 
position. A comparable business in the US or in Western Europe 
might trade at more like 30 times earnings, whereas Kaspi is trading 
at around 9 times trailing earnings, largely reflecting the geographic 
exposure to Kazakhstan. Could you briefly introduce the company 
for those unfamiliar with it? How do you assess the company risk 
premium embedded in its valuation, both in Kazakhstan specifically 
and when investing in emerging markets like Turkey in general? 
 
Pg. 8 of 14 
Mohnish: 
We talked about the Nifty 50, and we talked about the 50 bets. We 
also talked about being Rip Van Winkle and going to sleep for 20 
years.  
 
The situation with Kaspi is that there are two or three Harvard 
Business School case studies on the founder of Kaspi. If you go on 
the HBS publishing website and pay $ 12 or $13, you can buy those 
case studies. I will not tell HBS if you make copies for yourself and 
violate their rules of use. That will be between us. You can download 
those cases for $10 to 12, maybe $40 spent in total, and you would 
get a history of the man who is the founder of Kaspi. You can also 
look at the track record of the founder of Kaspi. I am studying the 
company. What they have done and what they have accomplished is 
remarkable. It is such an outlier, an extreme result. It is a great story. 
If you read those HBS cases, he took a failing bank and he converted 
it into a thriving fintech. They have 15 million users in Kazakhstan out 
of a population of about 20 million. They are pretty much a 
monopoly, a dominant player, like Tencent is in China.  
 
If you go on YouTube or to God Google, you can pull up some 
interviews he has given. He wants to get to 100 million users. He has 
entered the Turkish market, and the company he bought has around 
10 million users. He also bought a bank in Turkey. They are trying to 
replicate the playbook. He plans to replicate this in multiple 
countries, not only Turkey. We do not know what the trajectory is. 
We know that the guy has an exceptional track record. The company 
is relatively cheap based on what is currently in place. There is a 
moonshot. We do not know whether the moonshot happens or does 
not happen. That does not matter.  
 
We have an investment in a company in Turkey, which is like the 
Costco of Turkey. That is almost like a venture investment. They only 
have two stores. We do not have a lot of tread marks. I met the guy 
who runs the company. I visited the two stores, and I was blown 
away by the economics of those stores and how mobbed they are 
with customers, with no parking and everything. I said, “Okay, let us 
make a bet on this guy,” because it was cheap at that time. They had 
$70 million of extra real estate, and the market cap was $70 million. 
The business was free. We own over 30% of that business now.  
 
I do not know what happens with Kaspi. I do not know what happens 
with the Turkish Costco. I also do not know what happens with 
Reysas in the future. But we make these bets. They seem to be 
asymmetric bets. If all of them work. then Mohnish is going to be on 
a different planet. But even if some of them work, or even one of 
them works, we are okay. We keep looking for needles in haystacks. 
Every one, two, or three years, we might find one, two, or three 
things, and then we will see if it is worthwhile to make a bet. That is 
the situation. 
 
Gowzican: 
Very interesting. My next question is: How do you think about 
position sizing? 
 
Pg. 9 of 14 
Mohnish: 
The position sizing question is a great question. When we look at the 
Walton family, which had 46% of Walmart when Walmart went public 
and something like 99% of their net worth in Walmart, from then till 
now, several helpers went to the Walton family and told them, “Dear 
Mr. and Mrs. Walton, all the kids of Sam Walton who own the stock, 
you are extremely concentrated in one company. It is extremely 
risky. Let us put together an asset allocation plan for you that will 
diversify your holdings.” The Walton family asked them to leave. They 
kept their shares. Walmart gives a dividend. The dividend might be 
$5 to $7 billion a year. They end up with $2 or $3 billion a year in 
dividends. It is enough to live on. One can live on about $3 billion a 
year if you have 34 brothers and sisters.  
 
If you go to Bentonville, Arkansas, which I would highly recommend 
as a place to go on vacation, the Walton family has dumped money 
into various civil projects there. They have transformed the place. 
Amazing bike paths, incredible museums that go toe-to-toe with the 
best museums in the world, walking paths, and infrastructure for the 
community to enjoy parks and soccer fields. They have transformed 
the place. Billions of dollars have gone into Bentonville, Arkansas. I 
wish I lived there. When I grow up, hopefully I will be living in 
Bentonville, Arkansas without having ever having owned a share of 
Walmart stock.  
 
The Walton family decided we do not need to diversify.  
 
Now we come to Pabrai Investment Funds, and we have three stocks 
in Turkey that make up like 65 or 70% of the funds I manage. These 
are not my funds. I have investors. I tell my investors, “Dear investors, 
Mohnish is not going to sell any of these things. He is not going to 
diversify.” In the end, if things work out properly, 95% may be Reysas. 
Reysas may be a $20 billion market cap. We may have $8 billion in 
Reysas out of $9 or $10 billion in assets at some point, hopefully. We 
are not going to be selling an undervalued asset so that we are 
diversified. I said, “You are dealing with a nutcase. Let me explain to 
you how you should deal with the nutcase. If you have less than 20% 
of your total net worth with me, you have nothing to worry about. 
Because what that means is you have no more than 10% of your net 
worth in one particular company, and 80% is outside of me. I cannot 
make you poor. Even if I tried, I cannot. If you have more than 20% 
with me, you can sell. You can redeem some of your interest and take 
it down to 20%.” I send this note to them every quarter, in case they 
forgot to read it one quarter. I have around 300 families invested with 
me. I get no phone calls. I get no emails. I get no pulse. They all seem 
to be extremely happy. I get no redemption requests. This is the way 
life is.  
 
If you go into the investment business and after 20 or 30 years, 90% 
of your portfolio is not in one stock, you have badly made a loss.  
 
Gowzican: 
Thank you. I see that a big part of your public ETF has a large bet on 
Constellation Software companies. What do you see in those 
companies that you think the market is missing? 
Pg. 10 of 14 
 
Mohnish: 
These are like the Kaspi and other bets in the sense that we do not 
know what is going to happen. We like the DNA. Constellation has a 
long track record that one can look at. Mark Leonard is a one-of-a-
kind leader who has transferred his DNA to the companies. They are 
exceptional capital allocators. That will continue in the future. After 
the AI threat, the stock got taken out back and shot. When that 
happened, I got interested because now it was relatively cheap 
versus where it had been historically trading. We make the bet like 
we make the Kaspi and the Turkish Costco bets. We do not know 
which ones work, how well they work, and which ones do not work. 
The most important thing is to set it and forget it. Do not make any 
changes. Sit there and let them do their thing. That is it. 
 
Gowzican: 
 
We have a question from Jakob Wilkin. 
 
Johnny: 
I am Johnny from Frankfurt, and I wanted to ask you about Reysas. I 
see that in the last quarter, you sold around 21 million shares, and you 
have spoken a lot about it now. I wanted to hear, now that you are 
an established investor, when people see you invest in a company in 
an emerging market, do you not think that part of the difference in 
the gain afterward is also other investors thinking that you have a 
good history? They will also put their money into the stock that you 
have chosen. Also, why did you decide to sell a bit of your position 
here now? 
 
Mohnish: 
Reysas has two companies. There is a holding company, Reysas 
Logistics, and there is a REIT called Reysas REIT. We used to own 
almost 33% of Reysas Logistics, the holding company. The founding 
family, subtly, gave us a hint, saying, “We cannot officially tell you 
anything about your holdings, but we would be more comfortable if 
your stake in the holding company was kept to a maximum of 30%.” 
I said, “Do you care how much of the REIT we own?” They said, “Not 
at all.” The holding company owns 62% of the REIT. Whoever controls 
the holding company controls the REIT. We used to have about 33% 
of the holding company and a little less than 5% of the REIT. 
Collectively, let us say 38%. Now we have 30% of the holding 
company and 11% odd of the REIT. We increased our overall stake. 
The tailgating that takes place that you are referring to: in the long 
run, stocks are weighing machines. They are not voting machines.  
We also have investments in other positions in Turkey and elsewhere 
where we do not have tailgating. Somehow the people think that this 
manager is good on investment A, but maybe not so good on 
investment B. In my opinion, the Reysas position going from $15 
million to $1.8 billion is not tailgating. It is a weighing machine 
because now they can sell the business in 5 minutes at $3 billion if 
they want to. That $3 billion is compounding at 15, 20, or 25% a year. 
In fact, from my point of view, the weighing machine has not fully 
kicked in. I believe that a business like Reysas should not be valued 
at a liquidation value of $3 billion. It should be valued at a premium 
to liquidation value because there is a compounding engine built in. 
If a business is compounding and has shown historic compounding 
at 15, 20, 25% a year for a long period of time, and the asset is worth 
Pg. 11 of 14 
$3 billion, an investor coming in should be willing to come in at $3.5 
or $4 billion if they believe that compounding will continue. In my 
opinion, Reysas is deeply undervalued.  
 
Also, one of the things that I am grateful for is that I mentioned that 
a business should not be sold until it is egregiously overvalued. I hope 
and pray that Reysas never gets egregiously overvalued because 
what would happen then is that compounding would get 
interrupted, which is terrible. Let us say, for example, Reysas has a 
$3 billion value, and let us say the market value tomorrow goes to $8 
billion. In my opinion, that is egregious. That is clearly in egregious 
territory. But I also know that the son is 41 years old. If he is allowed 
to run this thing for 30 or 40 years, compounding at 15% or 20% a 
year, the value of that business may be well beyond $8 billion in that 
period of time. It is possible to be $20, $30, $40 billion, and we sell at 
$8 billion; we pay taxes, and then we get to find something else. That 
would be a terrible outcome. With Reysas, what has happened is that 
it has become clear to me that God truly loves me because what God 
has done is keep the value below liquidation value. When it is below 
liquidation value, it is the easiest stock to hold.  
 
The Walton family holding Walmart has a difficult job because they 
look at a stock that is at trailing earnings of 25. Is that undervalued? I 
am not sure. Is it overvalued? Maybe. Is it fairly valued? Maybe. I do 
not know where it is. What I am saying is that it is a harder thing to 
value. This has been so easy to hold for 7 years because it has always 
been below liquidation value. I hope it always stays there because if 
its liquidation value goes to $5 billion and the market cap is $3 billion, 
what do I do? Keep it. Liquidation value $10 billion, market cap $7 
billion. Keep it. I hope it does not go the other way because it is the 
easiest thing to keep. That is how I think about the business. I do not 
think the market is driven by the court tailors and all that. In the end, 
it is a weighing machine. 
 
Gowzican: 
 
Thanks. Mohnish. We have one last question from Anthony.  
 
Anthony: 
Thank you for taking the time to speak with us. My question is 
predicated on the idea that, as you say, the long-run returns should 
equate to the returns the business earns itself. To get better at 
finding these Costcos, I think it goes to also getting better at 
understanding these return dynamics. It could be quite interesting 
to hear your perspective on how you look at return on capital, 
especially on the incremental level.  
 
I think a good example is one of my good friends here as well, Miguel. 
We have been looking at this company that we think is doing about 
a 50% return on the capital that has been deployed, and they are 
reinvesting about half of that. With that math, they should be 
growing at maybe 20%. But when we look at the hub business itself, 
we think it is growing probably closer to high single digits or low 
double digits. That obviously creates a difference in the expected 
growth rate compared to what they are doing, indicating that either 
we have overestimated the returns or that the incremental level is 
Pg. 12 of 14 
much lower. But we do not see a clear business reason for why that 
should be occurring. It will be interesting to hear how you think 
about and how you approach understanding the underlying business 
economics and also how you try to look at it from an incremental 
perspective, which is where the compounding aspect kicks in. 
 
Mohnish: 
If a business is within your circle of competence, then it should be 
obvious to you how that business works and what kind of returns are 
coming out of the capital that is going into the business. If the 
retained earnings are being redeployed, what is the end result of 
those retained earnings on the business? Of course, things do not go 
in a straight line, and there can be mistakes. You have to look at this 
over some period of time.

they have done and individual things they have done and how they 
think about it, it has been truly exceptional in the sense that the error 
rates they have had are almost close to zero. I have not been able to 
find situations where they have outright lost a lot of money or made 
a dumb bet. On the other hand, there is deal after deal after deal 
where the returns on equity are 25% to 35%. We have also seen how 
the business has compounded value. The value of the business has 
gone from $800 million to $3 billion over a period of 7 years. That is 
a healthy rate of compounding over that period.  
 
I would say that when we look at a business like Kaspi, it is a digital 
business. The founders own around 43 or 44%, and they have created 
a lot of value. They are pumping out high dividends and investing in 
growth. Those guys are smart operators, and if the bets work, the 
returns are going to come out, and all will be fine.  
 
At the end of the day, when you look at these companies, you have 
to do your own analysis—you cannot take what the company is saying 
that we generate X return, Y return. You have to do your own analysis 
based on the trailing numbers and seeing what you are seeing. What 
you are seeing in those financials will give you a real view.

doing right from the beginning, and even now, is reinvesting ahead 
of the curve in a major way. He was not forthcoming about what he 
was doing, partially for competitive reasons. What you would see 
with Amazon was almost no net income. For the first 10, 15, 20 years, 
they had almost no net income. Jeff knew that the company was 
making money, but he was reinvesting at an aggressive rate. He was 
also making a lot of small bets where if the bet did not work, it was 
irrelevant, but if it worked, it was a big deal. When you looked at 
financials for a company like Amazon, from the financials, you would 
not be able to figure out that this is a truly exceptional business. It 
became visible over time when those bets started paying off, and he 
could not keep them under the radar. Eventually, AWS came out of 
the radar and started to go, but they are continuing to invest.

We are not always going to be able to look at the financials of a 
business and be able to figure out what is going on, if that business 
is prudently, carefully investing ahead of the curve, and they are 
investing in a myriad of businesses outside their core business. 
 
But it is a good journey. The good news is we are in a business with 
high error rates. If you make each bet a 10% bet, and you make 10 
bets, at the end of the day, you only need one of them to work 
extremely well. That is a great place to be.

Thank you, Mohnish. We are running out of time. The final question 
is: I know you have spent a lot of time with Charlie Munger. I would 
like to know what the lesson you have learned from him that has the 
most impact on your life?

Charlie and Warren are both friends. Charlie was a much closer friend 
than Warren because we were in the same city. With both men, the 
body of work that they have in the public domain is so vast that we 
can learn tremendous amounts from them without ever interacting 
with them. That is awesome. We do not need to have a relationship 
with them.  
 
Most of the things I learned from Charlie were not things he said to 
me. They were things I learned from observing him: observing how 
he was interacting with his kids, his grandkids, his daughter-in-law, 
his manservant, his business partners, and his friends. I learned from 
seeing how he lived his life on a day-to-day basis. I would go to his 
place and see how he was living his life. There were tremendous 
amounts of lessons that I learned from Charlie about that. I would 
notice, for example, the belt that Charlie wore on his waist had been 
worn out more than 10 or 15 years ago. It had gone well past its life. 
The guy is a multibillionaire. He could easily buy another belt, but it 
was not relevant to him. I would go see him, and he was wearing a 
Costco flannel shirt. You can buy those shirts at Costco for $10. I had 
asked him about that. He loved those shirts. I saw a person who was 
extremely wealthy, but who did not see any reason to frivolously use 
his wealth.  
 
Buffett said that eventually they were able to convince Charlie to get 
a share of NetJets. Buffett said it was a tough sale to get Charlie to 
buy NetJets for private flying. I talked to Charlie about that. I said, 
“Charlie, you have talked to me about how you love being on 
Southwest Airlines, middle seat and coach in the back of the plane.” 
It does not bother him at all. He is a big guy. He says, “Mohnish, I was 
fishing in Costa Rica, and at the end of the trip I was going to fly back, 
and I had commercial flight tickets. I had a bad headache. I called 
NetJets, and $80,000 later I was home.” He decided that it would be 
a higher quality of life for him at that point to ignore the commercial 
flight he was going to take and take NetJets straight home because 
he had a headache. I thought that was a prudent use of money by 
him. Not buying the belt was also a prudent use of money. It did not 
make any difference to him. It was interesting to calibrate how he 
thought about expenditures and money. 
Pg. 14 of 14 
 
Gowzican: 
 
Thank you, Mohnish. 
 
Mohnish: 
I wish you all the best, and I hope you have a good time, and please 
pursue looking for needles in haystacks. If you find the right needle, 
your entire life trajectory and your entire future gene pool are 
changed permanently.

Copenhagen Business School on August 25, 2026

Gowzican: 
We are so excited to have you here. My name is Gowzican. I am 
speaking on behalf of the CBS Investment Club at Copenhagen 
Business School. The CBS Investment Club is a club run by students. 
It is an investment fund focused on Nordic equities—gathering 
students from across the university interested in the markets and 
capital allocation. For those of you who do not know Mohnish, he is 
the founder and managing partner of Pabrai Investment Funds. He is 
also the CEO of Dhandho Funds and the author of The Dhandho 
Investor. Moreover, he has some philanthropic activities. He is the 
chairman and founder of the Dakshana Foundation, where he gives 
impoverished children in India opportunities to study at IIT, which is 
equivalent to MIT in the US. Mohnish, let us go straight to the Q&A 
session. 
 
My first question for you is: What advice do you have for students 
who want to go into the investment management business and try 
to emulate maybe what Buffett has done? 
 
Mohnish: 
The first thing I would suggest is that you need to have solid evidence 
that you are a good investor and that you are likely to be a good 
steward for other people's hard-earned money.  
 
The best way to accomplish that is to have an auditable track record 
that you have built over a few years with your own funds. What I 
would recommend is to have a brokerage account that is dedicated, 
where you are not writing checks here and there, but where, later at 
some point, that account can be handed over to an audit firm and 
they can relatively easily come up with an audited record of what the 
returns have been. The first thing is that there should be some 
reasonable period of time (5, 10 years or something) where you have 
built a record and you convinced yourself that you are good at this, 
and then after that if that goes well, you go on to convince folks to 
give you money to manage. On that front, you put your energies 
behind friends, family, and fools—and the most important are the 
fools. 
 
Gowzican: 
Interesting. My next question for you is: How do you deal with 
management when researching a company? They are often good at 
sales and charismatic people. How do you manage that?

Gowzican：
我们非常高兴能邀请您来这里。我叫 Gowzican，代表哥本哈根商学院的 CBS 投资俱乐部发言。CBS 投资俱乐部是一个由学生运营的社团，也是一只专注于北欧股票的投资基金，汇聚了全校对市场和资本配置感兴趣的学生。对于还不了解莫尼什的朋友，他是帕伯莱投资基金（Pabrai Investment Funds）的创始人兼管理合伙人。他也是 Dhandho Funds 的首席执行官，以及《Dhandho 投资者》（The Dhandho Investor）的作者。此外，他还从事一些慈善活动。他是达克希纳基金会（Dakshana Foundation）的主席兼创始人，为印度贫困儿童提供进入印度理工学院（IIT）学习的机会；印度理工学院相当于美国的麻省理工学院（MIT）。莫尼什，我们直接进入问答环节吧。

我的第一个问题是：对于希望进入投资管理行业，并尝试效仿巴菲特成就的学生，您有什么建议？

莫尼什：
我的第一条建议是，你需要有扎实的证据，证明自己是一名优秀的投资者，并且有望妥善管理别人辛辛苦苦挣来的钱。

做到这一点，最好的办法就是用自己的资金，在几年时间里积累一份可以审计的投资业绩记录。我建议开设一个专门的证券账户，不要用它到处开支票，这样将来的某个时候，就可以把这个账户交给一家审计机构，让他们相对容易地审计出你的回报记录。第一件事就是用一段合理的时间，比如 5 年、10 年之类，积累业绩记录，让自己确信擅长做这件事。如果一切顺利，之后再去说服别人把钱交给你管理。在这方面，你要把精力放在朋友、家人和傻瓜身上——其中最重要的是傻瓜。

Gowzican：
很有意思。我的下一个问题是：您在研究一家公司时，如何与管理层打交道？他们往往很善于推销，也很有个人魅力。您如何应对这一点？

investment was made around 2017, and we exited in 2023. I do not

person also reacted, and then pricing went down and got more 
aggressive. You end up with markets where normally having a Coke

put 2% of the portfolio into Walmart. Let us assume that the people 
who invested in the Nifty 50 did not touch it or sell it in the '73, '74 
downturn or from then until now. They kept the whole thing and did 
not make any trades. Let us also make an extreme assumption that 
every holding in that Nifty 50 went to zero except Walmart. You 
made an investment in a portfolio of 50 stocks. 49 stocks have gone 
to zero, and only one stock that you bought, which is Walmart, does 
what it did. If you looked at the returns from 1972, when Walmart 
went public, to 2026 (54 years), including reinvested dividends, 
Walmart has delivered about 15 or 16% a year annualized, and the S&P 
500, 15 or 16% a year. Starting with 2%, what I am saying is that with 
that 98% going to zero and the S&P having the entire 100 cents, the 
Nifty 50 portfolio with a 98% error rate blew out the S&P by about 5% 
a year, with 49 out of 50 stocks going to zero. 
 
Now, of course, 49 out of 50 stocks did not go to zero. We still have 
McDonald's, AMEX, Coke, and a lot of the other businesses. But many 
of the stocks did go to zero, like Xerox, Kodak, Polaroid, and Digital 
Equipment. But it did not matter. The bottom line was that one 
holding was enough to offset all the other losses. If we study stock 
markets for a long period of time, let us say over the last 100 years, 
for example, the US markets, what we find is that all the returns of 
the equity markets have come from 4% of the stocks. The remaining 
96% of the stocks have done nothing. They have gone to zero or done 
nothing. All the returns (that 9, 10, 11% a year that we get) have come 
from 4% of the equities. The important thing was not to buy Walmart. 
The important thing was not to touch Walmart, to never sell it, no 
matter what was happening, no matter what the company said and 
what they reported. You kept it.  
 
The Walton family owned 46% of Walmart when it went public in 
1972. After 54 years, they own more than 46% of Walmart. The Walton 
family has never sold Walmart in 54 years. Because Walmart has 
bought back shares, they own a higher percentage of the company. 
They followed that principle of holding, but no institutional investors 
held Walmart for 54 years.  
 
The important thing with investing is what Charlie Munger said is, in 
a lifetime, we are going to get a few trips to the pie counter. When 
we get a trip to the pie counter, we have to load up on a lot of pie 
and then try not to drop that pie till you get back to your table. 
Someone asked him once, “How can one be good at selling?” His 
response was, “Do not worry about becoming good at selling. Worry 
about becoming good at finding Costco's.”  
 
We can be useless at selling. We can sell nothing. We can have a high 
error rate, as long as we recognize that something in our portfolio is 
truly exceptional. It could be a small part of the portfolio like Walmart 
at 2%. But when we find ourselves in the lucky situation of partial 
ownership of a great business, do not sell that business because it 
looks fully priced. Do not sell that business when it looks overpriced.

looks fully priced. Do not sell that business when it looks overpriced.

假设：沃尔玛属于“漂亮 50”，而且有人将投资组合的 2% 投入了沃尔玛。再假设，那些投资“漂亮 50”的人，在 1973 年、1974 年的下跌期间，以及从那时到现在，都没有动过或卖出这些投资。他们一直完整持有，没有进行任何交易。我们再作一个极端的假设：“漂亮 50”中的每一只持仓都归零了，只有沃尔玛例外。你投资了一个由 50 只股票组成的组合。49 只股票已经归零，只有你买入的那只沃尔玛，取得了它实际取得的表现。如果看从沃尔玛上市的 1972 年到 2026 年这 54 年间的回报，包括股息再投资，沃尔玛的年化回报率约为 15% 或 16%，而标普 500 指数也是每年 15% 或 16%。从 2% 的初始仓位起步，我的意思是，尽管那 98% 都归零了，而标普投入的整整 100 美分都还在，这个错误率高达 98% 的“漂亮 50”投资组合，仍以每年约 5% 的优势大幅跑赢标普指数，哪怕 50 只股票中有 49 只归零。

当然，实际上并不是 50 只股票里有 49 只归零。麦当劳、美国运通、可口可乐和其他很多企业仍然存在。但确实有很多股票归零，比如施乐、柯达、宝丽来和数字设备公司（Digital Equipment）。不过，这并不重要。关键在于，一只持仓就足以抵消其他所有损失。如果我们长期研究股票市场，比如研究过去 100 年的美国市场，就会发现，股票市场的全部回报都来自 4% 的股票。其余 96% 的股票没有贡献什么。它们不是归零，就是毫无建树。所有的回报，也就是我们每年获得的 9%、10%、11%，都来自那 4% 的股票。重要的不是买入沃尔玛，重要的是不要动沃尔玛，永远不要卖出它，不管发生什么，不管公司说什么、发布了什么报告。你都要继续持有。

1972 年沃尔玛上市时，沃尔顿家族持有公司 46% 的股份。54 年之后，他们持有的沃尔玛股份超过了 46%。沃尔顿家族在这 54 年里从未卖出过沃尔玛。由于沃尔玛回购了股票，他们对公司的持股比例提高了。他们遵循了持有的原则，但没有任何机构投资者持有沃尔玛长达 54 年。

投资中重要的是查理·芒格说过的这件事：在一生中，我们会有几次走到馅饼柜台前的机会。当我们有机会走到馅饼柜台前，就得装上很多馅饼，然后尽量不要在回到自己桌子之前把馅饼掉在地上。有人曾经问他：“怎样才能善于卖出？”他的回答是：“不要费心去变得善于卖出。要费心去变得善于找到像 Costco 这样的公司。”

我们可以完全不擅长卖出。我们可以什么也不卖。我们可以有很高的错误率，只要我们能认识到，投资组合中有某个东西确实非同一般。它可以只是组合里很小的一部分，比如占比 2% 的沃尔玛。但是，当我们幸运地拥有一家伟大企业的部分所有权时，不要因为它看起来已经充分反映价值，就卖掉这家企业。也不要因为它看起来估值偏高，就卖掉这家企业。

If that business possibly gets egregiously overpriced, one could think 
about selling it.  
 
In 2018, I had noticed that the Turkish stock market was screening 
ultra-cheap. In fact, the cheapest in the world. I do not know 
anything about Turkey, like I know nothing about Copenhagen. But I 
have a good friend in Istanbul, who is now the second-largest equity 
fund manager in Turkey. He is a Ben Graham disciple. I told him, “I 
would love to visit Turkey, and I would love to visit the companies in 
your portfolio. Would you be open to that?” He said, “Oh, this would 
be a lot of fun, Mohnish. It would be great.” I made a trip to Turkey 
with nothing in mind other than trying to learn a bit more about this 
alien market and alien place. He sent me a list of companies that we 
were going to visit, and I never looked at the companies or studied 
them. I said that I would look at the businesses after I had met with 
them. If I met with the company and I saw something that looked 
interesting, then I would start doing research on them. What I was 
doing was that when we were driving to the business, I would start 
asking my friend questions about the business. I did not appear total 
village idiot at the meeting. I at least knew something about the 
business.  
 
The second year I visited Turkey in 2019, we were driving to this 
company, and I started asking my friend questions about it. He said, 
“The market cap is $15 million, and the liquidation value is $800 
million.” I asked him if this was a fraud. He said, “No, it is not a fraud. 
It is a simple, basic company. They rent warehouses, and I own the 
business. I have a stake in the business.” I asked him why it was so 
cheap. He said, “Well, everything in Turkey is cheap.” I had visited 
companies with him where the P/E was 0.1 (not a P/E of one; P/E of 
0.1). The company is trading at 1 month’s earnings. I had seen extreme 
stuff in Turkey.  
 
When he told me everything in Turkey is cheap, I shrugged. He is 
right. Everything in Turkey is cheap because no one is interested. 
Currency is unstable; inflation is out of control, all of this stuff.  
 
I met the company's founders, the father and son who run it. They 
seem like smart business people. I visited the warehouses that 
afternoon. They looked spectacular. They were prime. Things were 
exactly like he was saying. He said you could go to any commercial 
real estate broker in Istanbul, show them the portfolio, and they 
would tell you the portfolio is worth a billion dollars. There is $200 
million of debt, so it is worth $800 million. The market cap is like $15 
million. I was concerned because I was managing about $600 or 
$700 million. How much stock can I get? It is such a small company. 
But Turkey is a market of gamblers with high trading volumes. 
Everyone buys stocks at 10 o'clock, and they sell at 3 o'clock, and they 
want to make 10%. That is their business model. Buy at 10 o'clock, sell 
at 3 o'clock, make 10%. Good luck with that.  
 
Buffett has a quote that the stock market is a mechanism to transfer 
wealth from the active to the inactive.

2018 年，我注意到，用筛选指标看，土耳其股市便宜得惊人。事实上，它是全球最便宜的。我对土耳其一无所知，就像我对哥本哈根一无所知一样。不过，我有一位好朋友住在伊斯坦布尔，现在他是土耳其第二大股票基金经理。他是本杰明·格雷厄姆的追随者。我对他说：“我很想去土耳其看看，也很想拜访你投资组合中的公司。你愿意这样安排吗？”他说：“哦，莫尼什，那一定很有意思。太好了。”我去了土耳其，心里没有别的打算，只是想多了解一点这个陌生的市场、陌生的地方。他给我发了一份我们要拜访的公司名单，我既没看过那些公司，也没研究它们。我说，等见过他们之后，再来看这些企业。如果会面时我看到了有意思的东西，我才会开始研究它们。我的做法是，在开车前往公司的路上，开始向这位朋友询问有关这家企业的问题。这样在会面时，我就不至于显得像个彻头彻尾的乡巴佬，至少对这家公司还有一些了解。

2019 年，我第二年访问土耳其时，我们正开车前往一家公司，我开始向朋友询问它的情况。他说：“它的市值是 1,500 万美元，清算价值是 8 亿美元。”我问他这是不是骗局。他说：“不是，不是骗局。这是一家简单、朴实的公司。他们出租仓库，我持有这家公司。我在这家公司有股份。”我问他为什么这么便宜。他说：“嗯，土耳其的所有东西都很便宜。”我和他一起拜访过市盈率只有 0.1 倍的公司，不是 1 倍，而是 0.1 倍。公司的交易价格相当于 1 个月的盈利。我在土耳其见过非常极端的情况。

当他告诉我土耳其什么都便宜时，我耸了耸肩。他说得对。土耳其什么都便宜，因为没有人感兴趣。货币不稳定，通胀失控，诸如此类。

我见到了公司的创始人，也就是经营这家公司的那对父子。他们看起来是很精明的生意人。当天下午，我去看了那些仓库。它们看起来棒极了，都是优质资产。情况与他说的完全一样。他说，你可以随便找一家伊斯坦布尔的商业地产经纪公司，把这组资产展示给他们看，他们都会告诉你，这组资产价值 10 亿美元。减去 2 亿美元的债务，净值就是 8 亿美元。而市值只有大约 1,500 万美元。我有些担心，因为我当时管理着大约 6 亿或 7 亿美元。我究竟能买到多少股票？这家公司实在太小了。但土耳其是一个充满赌徒的市场，交易量很高。所有人都在上午 10 点买股票，下午 3 点卖出，希望赚 10%。这就是他们的商业模式。10 点买，3 点卖，赚 10%。那就祝他们好运吧。

巴菲特说过一句话：股市是一种将财富从活跃者手中转移到不活跃者手中的机制。

When I started buying the Reysas shares, I saw that the volumes 
were extremely high. The average public company in Turkey cycles 
through its float every 17 days, with high trading volumes because it 
is all gamblers and day traders. For $8 million, I got 1/3 of the 
company. I bought some more, and now we have a little over 41% of 
the company. The market cap of the company now is $1.8 billion 
dollars. The $15 million market cap in 2019 is a $1.8 billion market cap 
in 2026. The Turkish lira, which was 5 liras to the dollar in 2019 when 
I was buying, is more than 48 liras to the dollar. The lira has collapsed. 
It has gone down by more than 90%. But in dollars, we have more 
than a 120x return in 7 years. 
 
What I did not realize when I was buying the business is that my plan 
was okay; it is worth $800 million. When it gets to $600 or $700 
million or something, we will sell it. From $15 million to $600 million 
is a pretty nice ride. I was fully aware that Turkey has high inflation 
and an unstable currency being devalued a lot. But I remembered 
this story. Someone had told me once about the Coca-Cola 
company. Someone said that, let us say there is a global 
thermonuclear event. All the nukes owned by all the countries in the 
world are set off. Out of 8 billion humans, 99% are dead and gone. 
We have $80 million humans left. Everything is decimated. Someone 
somewhere creates a Coke bottling plant to start producing Coke for 
his fellow $80 million citizens. There is no currency. But people 
would be willing to trade 15 minutes of their labor for an 8-ounce 
serving of Coke. It does not matter if the currency is seashells or lira 
or dollars or cigarettes. There will be a trade available for one 
cigarette for a Coke or something like that. The Coke business would 
come back to serve the $80 million. Regardless of the currency, they 
had figured out the currencies.  
 
When I looked at the Turkish warehouse business, I thought, “What 
is a warehouse? A warehouse is land, cement, steel, concrete, and 
some paint. That is what a warehouse is.” Every one of those things

当我开始买入 Reysas 的股票时，我发现成交量极高。土耳其的上市公司平均每 17 天，流通股就会全部换手一次。成交量很高，因为市场里都是赌徒和日内交易者。我花了 800 万美元，就买到了这家公司三分之一的股份。后来我又买了一些，现在我们持有这家公司略高于 41% 的股份。这家公司现在的市值是 18 亿美元。2019 年 1,500 万美元的市值，到 2026 年变成了 18 亿美元。2019 年我买入时，土耳其里拉的汇率是 5 里拉兑 1 美元，现在则是超过 48 里拉兑 1 美元。里拉崩溃了，跌幅超过 90%。但以美元计，我们在 7 年里获得了超过 120 倍的回报。

买入这家企业时，我没有意识到后来会发生什么。当时我的计划是：好吧，它值 8 亿美元。等它涨到 6 亿、7 亿美元之类的水平，我们就卖掉。从 1,500 万美元到 6 亿美元，已经是一段相当不错的旅程了。我非常清楚，土耳其通胀高企，货币不稳定，而且在大幅贬值。但我想起了一个故事。有人曾经跟我讲过可口可乐公司的一个例子。那个人说，假设发生了一场全球性的热核事件，世界各国拥有的所有核武器都被引爆了。80 亿人中，99% 都死了，不复存在。剩下 8,000 万人。一切都遭到毁灭。某个地方的某个人建起了一家可口可乐装瓶厂，开始为剩下的 8,000 万同胞生产可乐。那时没有货币，但人们愿意用 15 分钟的劳动，换取一份 8 盎司的可乐。货币是贝壳、里拉、美元还是香烟，都无关紧要。人们总能用一支香烟换一瓶可乐，或者进行类似的交易。可口可乐的生意会重新出现，为那 8,000 万人提供服务。不管用什么货币，他们总能解决货币的问题。

当我看那家土耳其仓储企业时，我想：“仓库是什么？仓库就是土地、水泥、钢材、混凝土，再加上一些油漆。仓库就是这些东西。”其中每一样都会自动随通胀调整。他们爱怎么折腾里拉都行。土地会需要更多里拉来买，油漆也会需要更多里拉来买。价格自然会变化，因为世界就是这样运作的。它会随里拉的变化而变化。对我来说，当我在伊斯坦布尔这样的世界一流城市买入优质仓库时，不管租金是多少，它自然就与通胀挂钩了。我一点也不担心。我专门寻找土耳其那些不受货币和通胀影响的企业。我说：“尽管来吧。每年 1,000% 的通胀，尽管来。我准备好了，尽管来。无论你想要什么程度的通胀，都放马过来，因为我持有的是硬资产，它们会作出相应的反应和调整。”于是我下了注。当时我没有意识到，经营这家企业的那对父子，是极其出色的资本配置者。如果看不到以美元或欧元计的回报，而且看不到全部投入在 2 年或 3 年内收回，他们就不会投入资本。他们的思考方式很简单。如果以美元或欧元计，年投资回报率不超过 25% 至 35%，他们就没兴趣。2019 年价值 8 亿美元的企业，现在价值 30 亿美元。我仍然可以用同样的方法计算。

I go to a broker in Istanbul and show the portfolio. They are going to 
say, “This portfolio is worth like $3.4 billion, and there is $400 million 
of debt.” The market cap is $1.8 billion. The liquidation value is $3 
billion. That $3 billion liquidation value is compounding at, let us say, 
15 to 30% a year.  
 
We had a trip to the pie counter, the first one being Micron. On the 
way back, the pie got dropped on the floor, and it was no longer 
edible. We were only able to get a double return on the money, and 
the rest of the pie was swept up in the garbage. But then there was 
a second trip to the pie counter. What am I supposed to do with 
Reysas in Turkey? What I should do is spend all my time talking to the 
students at the Copenhagen Business School and leave the Reysas 
position alone. Like Charlie says, “Do not interrupt compounding 
unnecessarily.” Now I manage a little more than $1.4 billion. The 
Reysas position is $500-$550 million.  
 
There are a few other irons in the fire that I do not think are going to 
zero. My main job description is to not do any trades. It is to sit there 
and watch the pie. Next month, I am going to Istanbul. I go to 
Istanbul once a year in September or October and meet with the 
founders of Reysas. They own 44% of the company. My investors and 
I own 41% of the company. I tell them, “This is our family business. 
Your family and my family. I know we did not start as business 
partners. I know that you are the founder, and we have subsequently 
bought in. We do not want any board seats. I do not need to tell you 
anything because anything I tell you about how to run the business 
would make the business worse. Because I am so stupid at 
everything and you are so good at everything.”  
 
We go eat blue fish at a Michelin-starred restaurant overlooking the 
Bosphorus. It is a nice dinner. I pat them on the back, and I say, “Keep 
doing what you are doing, and I will see you next year.” That is my job 
description. We are done. I hope they stay in the saddle, and I hope 
they run that business for 20, 30, 40 years or more. Recently, I have 
noticed that the son has been bringing his 11-year-old son to various 
business meetings. I said, “Amen.” Let us get the next generation 
ready so that after 40 years, the compounding can continue.  
 
Gowzican: 
Interesting, Mohnish. We have a question from Will Hansen, who is 
also a member of the Investment Club. His question is: One of your 
most recent investments is Kaspi in Kazakhstan, which appears to be 
an exceptional business. With a strong management team, high 
growth, excellent margins, and a monopoly-like competitive 
position. A comparable business in the US or in Western Europe 
might trade at more like 30 times earnings, whereas Kaspi is trading 
at around 9 times trailing earnings, largely reflecting the geographic 
exposure to Kazakhstan. Could you briefly introduce the company 
for those unfamiliar with it? How do you assess the company risk 
premium embedded in its valuation, both in Kazakhstan specifically 
and when investing in emerging markets like Turkey in general?

我去找伊斯坦布尔的一位经纪人，把这组资产展示给他。他会说：“这组资产大概值 34 亿美元，另有 4 亿美元的债务。”市值是 18 亿美元，清算价值是 30 亿美元。而这 30 亿美元的清算价值，正以每年比如 15% 至 30% 的速度复利增长。

我们曾有机会走到馅饼柜台前，第一次是美光。回来的路上，馅饼掉到了地上，不能再吃了。我们的钱只翻了一倍，剩下的馅饼都被扫进垃圾桶了。但后来，我们又获得了第二次走到馅饼柜台前的机会。对于土耳其的 Reysas，我应该做什么？我应该把所有时间都用来和哥本哈根商学院的学生交流，而不要去动 Reysas 的持仓。就像查理说的：“不要无谓地打断复利。”现在，我管理的资金略高于 14 亿美元。Reysas 持仓的价值是 5 亿至 5.5 亿美元。

我还在做其他几项投资，我认为它们不会归零。我的主要工作职责就是不做任何交易。坐在那里，看好馅饼。下个月，我要去伊斯坦布尔。我每年 9 月或 10 月都会去一次，见见 Reysas 的创始人。他们持有公司 44% 的股份，我和我的投资者持有 41%。我对他们说：“这是我们的家族企业，你们家和我们家的企业。我知道，我们一开始并不是商业伙伴。我知道，你们是创始人，而我们是后来买入的。我们不想要任何董事会席位。我不需要给你们任何意见，因为如果我告诉你们该怎么经营，这家企业只会变得更糟。因为我什么都那么蠢，而你们什么都那么擅长。”

我们会去一家俯瞰博斯普鲁斯海峡的米其林星级餐厅吃蓝鱼。那是一顿很棒的晚餐。我拍拍他们的背，说：“继续做你们正在做的事，我们明年见。”这就是我的工作职责。我们的事就办完了。我希望他们继续掌舵，希望他们再经营这家企业 20 年、30 年、40 年，甚至更久。最近，我注意到，儿子开始带着他 11 岁的儿子参加各种商务会议。我说：“阿门。”让我们把下一代培养好，这样 40 年之后，复利还能继续。

Gowzican：
很有意思，莫尼什。我们收到一个来自 Will Hansen 的问题，他也是投资俱乐部的成员。他的问题是：您最近的投资之一，是哈萨克斯坦的 Kaspi。这似乎是一家非同一般的企业，拥有强大的管理团队、高增长、出色的利润率，以及近乎垄断的竞争地位。美国或西欧的同类企业，市盈率可能超过 30 倍，而 Kaspi 目前的历史市盈率大约为 9 倍，很大程度上反映了其对哈萨克斯坦的地域敞口。您能否为不熟悉它的人简要介绍一下这家公司？您如何评估其估值中包含的公司风险溢价，既包括哈萨克斯坦的具体情况，也包括更广泛地投资土耳其等新兴市场的情况？

莫尼什：
我们谈到了“漂亮 50”，谈到了那 50 次下注。我们也谈到了像瑞普·凡·温克尔那样，一觉睡上 20 年。

Kaspi 的情况是，哈佛商学院有两三篇关于 Kaspi 创始人的案例研究。你去哈佛商学院出版社的网站，花 12 或 13 美元，就能买到那些案例。如果你给自己复印，违反了他们的使用规定，我不会向哈佛商学院告发你。这件事就你知我知。花 10 至 12 美元就能下载那些案例，也许总共花 40 美元，你就能了解 Kaspi 创始人的经历。你也可以看看 Kaspi 创始人的过往业绩。我正在研究这家公司。他们所做的事情、取得的成就，非常了不起。这是一个极其罕见的异数，一个极端出色的结果。这是个很棒的故事。如果你读过那些哈佛商学院案例，就会看到，他把一家濒临失败的银行，转变成了一家蓬勃发展的金融科技企业。哈萨克斯坦的人口大约有 2,000 万，他们在那里拥有 1,500 万用户。他们基本上处于垄断地位，是一家占据主导地位的企业，就像腾讯在中国一样。

如果你去 YouTube，或者求助于“谷歌大神”，就能找到他接受的一些访谈。他想把用户数做到 1 亿。他已经进入土耳其市场，收购的那家公司大约有 1,000 万用户。他还在土耳其买了一家银行。他们正试图复制这套打法。他计划在多个国家复制，而不只是土耳其。我们不知道未来的发展轨迹。我们知道，这个人有极其出色的历史业绩。按照目前已经具备的业务来看，这家公司相对便宜。另外还有一个登月般的远大目标。我们不知道这个目标能否实现，但这并不重要。

我们投资了土耳其的一家公司，它就像土耳其的 Costco。这几乎像是一笔风险投资。他们只有两家门店，我们没有多少过往记录可供参考。我见过经营这家公司的人，也去过那两家门店。那些门店的经济效益，以及顾客多到挤得水泄不通、连车都无处停的景象，让我大为震撼。我说：“好吧，让我们在这个人身上下个注。”因为那时候它很便宜。他们拥有价值 7,000 万美元的额外房地产，而公司的市值也是 7,000 万美元。经营业务相当于白送。现在我们持有这家企业超过 30% 的股份。

我不知道 Kaspi 会怎样。我不知道土耳其的 Costco 会怎样。我也不知道 Reysas 将来会怎样。但我们会下注。这些看起来都是风险收益不对称的下注。如果它们全都成功，莫尼什就要飞到另一个星球去了。但即使只有其中一些成功，甚至只有一个成功，我们也没问题。我们会继续在干草堆里找针。每隔一年、两年或三年，我们可能会找到一件、两件或三件东西，再看看是否值得下注。情况就是这样。

Mohnish: 
The position sizing question is a great question. When we look at the 
Walton family, which had 46% of Walmart when Walmart went public 
and something like 99% of their net worth in Walmart, from then till 
now, several helpers went to the Walton family and told them, “Dear 
Mr. and Mrs. Walton, all the kids of Sam Walton who own the stock, 
you are extremely concentrated in one company. It is extremely 
risky. Let us put together an asset allocation plan for you that will 
diversify your holdings.” The Walton family asked them to leave. They 
kept their shares. Walmart gives a dividend. The dividend might be 
$5 to $7 billion a year. They end up with $2 or $3 billion a year in 
dividends. It is enough to live on. One can live on about $3 billion a 
year if you have 34 brothers and sisters.  
 
If you go to Bentonville, Arkansas, which I would highly recommend 
as a place to go on vacation, the Walton family has dumped money 
into various civil projects there. They have transformed the place. 
Amazing bike paths, incredible museums that go toe-to-toe with the 
best museums in the world, walking paths, and infrastructure for the 
community to enjoy parks and soccer fields. They have transformed 
the place. Billions of dollars have gone into Bentonville, Arkansas. I 
wish I lived there. When I grow up, hopefully I will be living in 
Bentonville, Arkansas without having ever having owned a share of 
Walmart stock.  
 
The Walton family decided we do not need to diversify.  
 
Now we come to Pabrai Investment Funds, and we have three stocks 
in Turkey that make up like 65 or 70% of the funds I manage. These 
are not my funds. I have investors. I tell my investors, “Dear investors, 
Mohnish is not going to sell any of these things. He is not going to 
diversify.” In the end, if things work out properly, 95% may be Reysas. 
Reysas may be a $20 billion market cap. We may have $8 billion in 
Reysas out of $9 or $10 billion in assets at some point, hopefully. We 
are not going to be selling an undervalued asset so that we are 
diversified. I said, “You are dealing with a nutcase. Let me explain to 
you how you should deal with the nutcase. If you have less than 20% 
of your total net worth with me, you have nothing to worry about. 
Because what that means is you have no more than 10% of your net 
worth in one particular company, and 80% is outside of me. I cannot 
make you poor. Even if I tried, I cannot. If you have more than 20% 
with me, you can sell. You can redeem some of your interest and take 
it down to 20%.” I send this note to them every quarter, in case they 
forgot to read it one quarter. I have around 300 families invested with 
me. I get no phone calls. I get no emails. I get no pulse. They all seem 
to be extremely happy. I get no redemption requests. This is the way 
life is.  
 
If you go into the investment business and after 20 or 30 years, 90% 
of your portfolio is not in one stock, you have badly made a loss.  
 
Gowzican: 
Thank you. I see that a big part of your public ETF has a large bet on 
Constellation Software companies. What do you see in those 
companies that you think the market is missing?

莫尼什：
仓位大小是一个很好的问题。看看沃尔顿家族：沃尔玛上市时，他们持有沃尔玛 46% 的股份，而且大约 99% 的净资产都在沃尔玛。从那时到现在，有不少想帮忙的人去找过沃尔顿家族，对他们说：“亲爱的沃尔顿先生和太太，以及萨姆·沃尔顿所有持有股票的孩子们，你们的财富极度集中在一家公司身上，风险极高。让我们为你们制定一份资产配置计划，分散你们的持仓。”沃尔顿家族请他们离开了。他们保留了自己的股票。沃尔玛会支付股息，每年的股息总额可能是 50 亿至 70 亿美元。他们最终每年能收到 20 亿或 30 亿美元的股息。这足够生活了。如果你有 34 个兄弟姐妹，每年大约 30 亿美元也能过日子。

如果你去阿肯色州的本顿维尔——我非常推荐大家把它作为度假目的地——就会看到，沃尔顿家族在那里向各种市政项目投入了大量资金。他们彻底改变了那个地方。那里有非常棒的自行车道、足以媲美世界顶级博物馆的出色博物馆、步行道，以及供社区居民享用公园和足球场的基础设施。他们改变了那个地方。数十亿美元投入了阿肯色州的本顿维尔。我真希望自己住在那里。等我长大以后，希望我能住在阿肯色州的本顿维尔，而我从来没有持有过哪怕一股沃尔玛股票。

沃尔顿家族作出的决定是：我们不需要分散投资。

现在说回帕伯莱投资基金。我们在土耳其持有三只股票，大约占我管理资金的 65% 或 70%。这些不是我自己的钱，我有投资者。我对投资者说：“亲爱的投资者，莫尼什不会卖出其中任何一项。他不会分散投资。”最后，如果一切进展顺利，Reysas 可能会占到 95%。Reysas 的市值可能达到 200 亿美元。希望在未来某个时点，我们 90 亿或 100 亿美元的资产中，会有 80 亿美元投在 Reysas 上。我们不会为了分散投资而卖出低估的资产。我说：“你们在和一个疯子打交道。让我解释一下，应该如何与这个疯子打交道。如果你交给我的钱不到你总净资产的 20%，就没有什么可担心的。因为这意味着，你投入某一家公司的净资产不会超过 10%，还有 80% 不在我这里。我没法让你变穷。即使我想这么做，也做不到。如果你交给我的钱超过了 20%，你可以卖出。你可以赎回一部分份额，把比例降到 20%。”我每个季度都会把这段话发给他们，免得他们某个季度忘了看。大约有 300 个家庭把钱交给我投资。我收不到电话，也收不到电子邮件，连一点动静都没有。他们似乎都非常开心。我也收不到赎回请求。日子就是这么过的。

如果你进入投资行业，20 年或 30 年之后，你投资组合的 90% 还没有集中在一只股票上，那你就亏大了。

仓位大小是一个很好的问题。看看沃尔顿家族：沃尔玛上市时，他们持有沃尔玛 46% 的股份，而且大约 99% 的净资产都在沃尔玛。从那时到现在，有不少想帮忙的人去找过沃尔顿家族，对他们说：“亲爱的沃尔顿先生和太太，以及萨姆·沃尔顿所有持有股票的孩子们，你们的财富极度集中在一家公司身上，风险极高。让我们为你们制定一份资产配置计划，分散你们的持仓。”沃尔顿家族请他们离开了。他们保留了自己的股票。沃尔玛会支付股息，每年的股息总额可能是 50 亿至 70 亿美元。他们最终每年能收到 20 亿或 30 亿美元的股息。这足够生活了。如果你有 34 个兄弟姐妹，每年大约 30 亿美元也能过日子。

如果你去阿肯色州的本顿维尔——我非常推荐大家把它作为度假目的地——就会看到，沃尔顿家族在那里向各种市政项目投入了大量资金。他们彻底改变了那个地方。那里有非常棒的自行车道、足以媲美世界顶级博物馆的出色博物馆、步行道，以及供社区居民享用公园和足球场的基础设施。他们改变了那个地方。数十亿美元投入了阿肯色州的本顿维尔。我真希望自己住在那里。等我长大以后，希望我能住在阿肯色州的本顿维尔，而我从来没有持有过哪怕一股沃尔玛股票。
沃尔顿家族作出的决定是：我们不需要分散投资。

现在说回帕伯莱投资基金。我们在土耳其持有三只股票，大约占我管理资金的 65% 或 70%。这些不是我自己的钱，我有投资者。我对投资者说：“亲爱的投资者，莫尼什不会卖出其中任何一项。他不会分散投资。”最后，如果一切进展顺利，Reysas 可能会占到 95%。Reysas 的市值可能达到 200 亿美元。希望在未来某个时点，我们 90 亿或 100 亿美元的资产中，会有 80 亿美元投在 Reysas 上。我们不会为了分散投资而卖出低估的资产。我说：“你们在和一个疯子打交道。让我解释一下，应该如何与这个疯子打交道。如果你交给我的钱不到你总净资产的 20%，就没有什么可担心的。因为这意味着，你投入某一家公司的净资产不会超过 10%，还有 80% 不在我这里。我没法让你变穷。即使我想这么做，也做不到。如果你交给我的钱超过了 20%，你可以卖出。你可以赎回一部分份额，把比例降到 20%。”我每个季度都会把这段话发给他们，免得他们某个季度忘了看。大约有 300 个家庭把钱交给我投资。我收不到电话，也收不到电子邮件，连一点动静都没有。他们似乎都非常开心。我也收不到赎回请求。日子就是这么过的。
如果你进入投资行业，20 年或 30 年之后，你投资组合的 90% 还没有集中在一只股票上，那你就亏大了。

These are like the Kaspi and other bets in the sense that we do not 
know what is going to happen. We like the DNA. Constellation has a 
long track record that one can look at. Mark Leonard is a one-of-a-
kind leader who has transferred his DNA to the companies. They are 
exceptional capital allocators. That will continue in the future. After 
the AI threat, the stock got taken out back and shot. When that 
happened, I got interested because now it was relatively cheap 
versus where it had been historically trading. We make the bet like 
we make the Kaspi and the Turkish Costco bets. We do not know 
which ones work, how well they work, and which ones do not work. 
The most important thing is to set it and forget it. Do not make any 
changes. Sit there and let them do their thing. That is it.

We have a question from Jakob Wilkin. 
 
Johnny: 
I am Johnny from Frankfurt, and I wanted to ask you about Reysas. I 
see that in the last quarter, you sold around 21 million shares, and you 
have spoken a lot about it now. I wanted to hear, now that you are 
an established investor, when people see you invest in a company in 
an emerging market, do you not think that part of the difference in 
the gain afterward is also other investors thinking that you have a 
good history? They will also put their money into the stock that you 
have chosen. Also, why did you decide to sell a bit of your position 
here now? 
 
Mohnish: 
Reysas has two companies. There is a holding company, Reysas 
Logistics, and there is a REIT called Reysas REIT. We used to own 
almost 33% of Reysas Logistics, the holding company. The founding 
family, subtly, gave us a hint, saying, “We cannot officially tell you 
anything about your holdings, but we would be more comfortable if 
your stake in the holding company was kept to a maximum of 30%.” 
I said, “Do you care how much of the REIT we own?” They said, “Not 
at all.” The holding company owns 62% of the REIT. Whoever controls 
the holding company controls the REIT. We used to have about 33% 
of the holding company and a little less than 5% of the REIT. 
Collectively, let us say 38%. Now we have 30% of the holding 
company and 11% odd of the REIT. We increased our overall stake. 
The tailgating that takes place that you are referring to: in the long 
run, stocks are weighing machines. They are not voting machines.  
We also have investments in other positions in Turkey and elsewhere 
where we do not have tailgating. Somehow the people think that this 
manager is good on investment A, but maybe not so good on 
investment B. In my opinion, the Reysas position going from $15 
million to $1.8 billion is not tailgating. It is a weighing machine

莫尼什：
这些与 Kaspi 以及其他下注类似，因为我们不知道将来会发生什么。我们喜欢它们的基因。星座软件有长期的业绩记录可供研究。马克·伦纳德（Mark Leonard）是一位独一无二的领导者，他已经把自己的基因传给了这些公司。他们是出色的资本配置者，未来也会如此。在人工智能的威胁出现之后，这只股票像是被拖到后院枪毙了一样。发生这种情况时，我就产生了兴趣，因为与历史交易水平相比，现在它已经相对便宜了。我们就像投资 Kaspi 和土耳其的 Costco 一样，下注投资它。我们不知道哪些会成功，成功到什么程度，哪些又不会成功。最重要的是，配置好之后就忘掉它。不要作任何改变。坐在那里，让它们去做自己的事。就这么简单。

我们有一个来自 Jakob Wilkin 的问题。

Johnny：
我叫 Johnny，来自法兰克福。我想问您一个关于 Reysas 的问题。我看到，上个季度您卖出了大约 2,100 万股，而刚才您也谈了很多这家公司。我想听听您的看法：现在您已经是一位成名的投资者，当人们看到您投资一家新兴市场的公司时，您是否认为，之后上涨幅度中的一部分，也来自其他投资者觉得您的历史业绩很好？他们也会把钱投进您选中的股票。另外，为什么您现在决定卖出这里的一小部分持仓？

莫尼什：
Reysas 有两家公司。一家是控股公司 Reysas Logistics，另一家是名为 Reysas REIT 的房地产投资信托基金。我们以前持有控股公司 Reysas Logistics 接近 33% 的股份。创始家族很委婉地向我们暗示：“对于你们的持股，我们不能正式说什么，但如果你们在控股公司的持股比例最高保持在 30%，我们会更安心。”我说：“你们在乎我们持有多少 REIT 的股份吗？”他们说：“完全不在乎。”控股公司持有 REIT 的 62%。谁控制了控股公司，谁就控制了 REIT。以前，我们持有控股公司大约 33% 的股份，以及 REIT 略低于 5% 的股份。加在一起，姑且说是 38%。现在，我们持有控股公司 30% 的股份，以及 REIT 大约 11% 多一点的股份。我们的总体持股增加了。至于你所说的跟风买入，从长期来看，股票是称重机，而不是投票机。
我们在土耳其以及其他地方还有别的投资，并没有出现这种跟风买入。不知为什么，人们觉得，这位基金经理在投资 A 上很在行，但在投资 B 上可能就没那么在行。在我看来，Reysas 这项投资从 1,500 万美元涨到 18 亿美元，不是跟风造成的，而是称重机在起作用。因为现在，只要他们愿意，就能在 5 分钟内以 30 亿美元的价格卖掉这家企业。那 30 亿美元正以每年 15%、20% 或 25% 的速度复利增长。事实上，在我看来，称重机还没有充分发挥作用。我认为，Reysas 这样的企业不应该仅按 30 亿美元的清算价值来估值。它的估值应该高于清算价值，因为里面有一台复利引擎。如果一家企业在进行复利增长，而且历史上已经长期展现出每年 15%、20%、25% 的复利增长，同时这项资产价值

Also, one of the things that I am grateful for is that I mentioned that

and pray that Reysas never gets egregiously overvalued because 
what would happen then is that compounding would get 
interrupted, which is terrible. Let us say, for example, Reysas has a 
$3 billion value, and let us say the market value tomorrow goes to $8 
billion. In my opinion, that is egregious. That is clearly in egregious 
territory. But I also know that the son is 41 years old. If he is allowed 
to run this thing for 30 or 40 years, compounding at 15% or 20% a 
year, the value of that business may be well beyond $8 billion in that 
period of time. It is possible to be $20, $30, $40 billion, and we sell at 
$8 billion; we pay taxes, and then we get to find something else. That 
would be a terrible outcome. With Reysas, what has happened is that 
it has become clear to me that God truly loves me because what God 
has done is keep the value below liquidation value. When it is below 
liquidation value, it is the easiest stock to hold.  
 
The Walton family holding Walmart has a difficult job because they 
look at a stock that is at trailing earnings of 25. Is that undervalued? I 
am not sure. Is it overvalued? Maybe. Is it fairly valued? Maybe. I do 
not know where it is. What I am saying is that it is a harder thing to 
value. This has been so easy to hold for 7 years because it has always 
been below liquidation value. I hope it always stays there because if 
its liquidation value goes to $5 billion and the market cap is $3 billion, 
what do I do? Keep it. Liquidation value $10 billion, market cap $7 
billion. Keep it. I hope it does not go the other way because it is the 
easiest thing to keep. That is how I think about the business. I do not 
think the market is driven by the court tailors and all that. In the end, 
it is a weighing machine.

另外，还有一件事让我心怀感激。我刚才说过，除非一家企业被高估得离谱，否则不应该卖出。我希望并祈祷，Reysas 永远不要被高估得离谱，因为如果真是那样，复利就会被打断，而那是很糟糕的。举个例子，假设 Reysas 的价值是 30 亿美元，又假设明天市值涨到了 80 亿美元。在我看来，这就高得离谱了。显然已经进入了离谱的区间。但我也知道，那位儿子现在 41 岁。如果让他再经营这家企业 30 年或 40 年，每年以 15% 或 20% 的速度复利增长，那么在这段时间里，这家企业的价值可能远远超过 80 亿美元，可能达到 200 亿、300 亿、400 亿美元。而我们在 80 亿美元时卖出，缴税，然后又得去找别的投资。那会是一个糟糕的结果。Reysas 的经历让我清楚地意识到，上帝真的爱我，因为上帝让它的市值始终低于清算价值。只要低于清算价值，它就是最容易持有的股票。

沃尔顿家族持有沃尔玛，其实是一件很难的事，因为他们面对的是一只历史市盈率为 25 倍的股票。这算低估吗？我不确定。算高估吗？也许。算合理估值吗？也许。我不知道它处于哪个位置。我的意思是，它更难估值。而这只股票在过去 7 年里一直很容易持有，因为它始终低于清算价值。我希望它一直如此。因为，如果它的清算价值达到 50 亿美元，市值是 30 亿美元，我该怎么做？继续持有。清算价值 100 亿美元，市值 70 亿美元。继续持有。我希望它不要反过来，因为这样最容易持有。这就是我看待这家企业的方式。我不认为市场是由那些跟风者之类的人推动的〔译注：原文作 court tailors，疑为 coattailers 的转录误写〕。最终，它是一台称重机。

谢谢你，莫尼什。我们还有最后一个来自 Anthony 的问题。

Anthony：
感谢您抽时间与我们交流。我的问题基于这样一个理念：正如您所说，长期投资回报应该等同于企业自身赚取的回报。为了更善于找到像 Costco 这样的公司，我认为也需要更善于理解这些回报的变化机制。我很想听听您如何看待资本回报率，尤其是增量层面的资本回报率。

Mohnish: 
If a business is within your circle of competence, then it should be 
obvious to you how that business works and what kind of returns are 
coming out of the capital that is going into the business. If the 
retained earnings are being redeployed, what is the end result of 
those retained earnings on the business? Of course, things do not go 
in a straight line, and there can be mistakes. You have to look at this 
over some period of time.  
 
When I look at a company like Reysas, and I look at individual deals 
they have done and individual things they have done and how they 
think about it, it has been truly exceptional in the sense that the error 
rates they have had are almost close to zero. I have not been able to 
find situations where they have outright lost a lot of money or made 
a dumb bet. On the other hand, there is deal after deal after deal 
where the returns on equity are 25% to 35%. We have also seen how 
the business has compounded value. The value of the business has 
gone from $800 million to $3 billion over a period of 7 years. That is 
a healthy rate of compounding over that period.  
 
I would say that when we look at a business like Kaspi, it is a digital 
business. The founders own around 43 or 44%, and they have created 
a lot of value. They are pumping out high dividends and investing in 
growth. Those guys are smart operators, and if the bets work, the 
returns are going to come out, and all will be fine.  
 
At the end of the day, when you look at these companies, you have 
to do your own analysis—you cannot take what the company is saying 
that we generate X return, Y return. You have to do your own analysis 
based on the trailing numbers and seeing what you are seeing. What 
you are seeing in those financials will give you a real view.  
 
Now, if you look at a business like Amazon, what Jeff Bezos was 
doing right from the beginning, and even now, is reinvesting ahead 
of the curve in a major way. He was not forthcoming about what he 
was doing, partially for competitive reasons. What you would see 
with Amazon was almost no net income. For the first 10, 15, 20 years, 
they had almost no net income. Jeff knew that the company was 
making money, but he was reinvesting at an aggressive rate. He was 
also making a lot of small bets where if the bet did not work, it was 
irrelevant, but if it worked, it was a big deal. When you looked at 
financials for a company like Amazon, from the financials, you would 
not be able to figure out that this is a truly exceptional business. It 
became visible over time when those bets started paying off, and he 
could not keep them under the radar. Eventually, AWS came out of 
the radar and started to go, but they are continuing to invest.

莫尼什：
如果一家企业处于你的能力圈内，那么，它如何运作，投入企业的资本会产生怎样的回报，对你来说都应该是显而易见的。如果留存收益被重新投入，这些留存收益最终对企业产生了什么结果？当然，事情不会沿着一条直线发展，也可能会犯错。你必须在一段时间内观察。

当我观察 Reysas 这样的公司，研究他们做过的一笔笔交易、一件件事情，以及他们的思考方式时，会发现他们确实非同一般，因为他们的错误率几乎接近于零。我找不到他们直接亏掉很多钱，或者做过愚蠢下注的情况。另一方面，我看到的是一笔接一笔、再接一笔净资产收益率达到 25% 至 35% 的交易。我们也看到了这家企业如何通过复利增长创造价值。7 年时间里，企业价值从 8 亿美元增长到了 30 亿美元。这段时期的复利增长率相当不错。

我想说的是，当我们看 Kaspi 这样的公司时，它是一家数字化企业。创始人持有大约 43% 或 44% 的股份，并且已经创造了大量价值。他们一边支付高额股息，一边为增长投资。这些人是精明的经营者。如果他们的下注成功，回报自然会显现，一切都会很好。

归根结底，在研究这些公司时，你必须自己分析，不能直接相信公司所说的“我们能创造 X 回报、Y 回报”。你必须根据历史数据，以及自己实际观察到的情况，作出独立分析。财务报表里呈现的内容，会让你看到真实的情况。

再看亚马逊这样的企业，杰夫·贝索斯从一开始就在做的事，甚至现在仍在做的事，就是大规模地超前再投资。他没有坦率公开自己在做什么，部分原因是竞争方面的考虑。你看到的亚马逊几乎没有净利润。最初的 10 年、15 年、20 年，他们几乎都没有净利润。杰夫知道公司在赚钱，但他在以非常激进的速度进行再投资。他还在做很多小额下注，失败了无关紧要，成功了却会产生重大影响。看亚马逊这样的公司，如果只看财务报表，你无法判断出这是一家真正非凡的企业。随着时间推移，当那些下注开始取得回报，而他再也无法让它们保持低调时，人们才逐渐看清这一点。最终，AWS 不再隐于雷达之下，开始腾飞，但他们仍然在继续投资。

We are not always going to be able to look at the financials of a 
business and be able to figure out what is going on, if that business 
is prudently, carefully investing ahead of the curve, and they are 
investing in a myriad of businesses outside their core business. 
 
But it is a good journey. The good news is we are in a business with 
high error rates. If you make each bet a 10% bet, and you make 10 
bets, at the end of the day, you only need one of them to work 
extremely well. That is a great place to be. 
 
Gowzican: 
Thank you, Mohnish. We are running out of time. The final question 
is: I know you have spent a lot of time with Charlie Munger. I would 
like to know what the lesson you have learned from him that has the 
most impact on your life? 
 
Mohnish: 
Charlie and Warren are both friends. Charlie was a much closer friend 
than Warren because we were in the same city. With both men, the 
body of work that they have in the public domain is so vast that we 
can learn tremendous amounts from them without ever interacting 
with them. That is awesome. We do not need to have a relationship 
with them.  
 
Most of the things I learned from Charlie were not things he said to 
me. They were things I learned from observing him: observing how 
he was interacting with his kids, his grandkids, his daughter-in-law, 
his manservant, his business partners, and his friends. I learned from 
seeing how he lived his life on a day-to-day basis. I would go to his 
place and see how he was living his life. There were tremendous 
amounts of lessons that I learned from Charlie about that. I would 
notice, for example, the belt that Charlie wore on his waist had been 
worn out more than 10 or 15 years ago. It had gone well past its life. 
The guy is a multibillionaire. He could easily buy another belt, but it 
was not relevant to him. I would go see him, and he was wearing a 
Costco flannel shirt. You can buy those shirts at Costco for $10. I had 
asked him about that. He loved those shirts. I saw a person who was 
extremely wealthy, but who did not see any reason to frivolously use 
his wealth.  
 
Buffett said that eventually they were able to convince Charlie to get 
a share of NetJets. Buffett said it was a tough sale to get Charlie to 
buy NetJets for private flying. I talked to Charlie about that. I said, 
“Charlie, you have talked to me about how you love being on 
Southwest Airlines, middle seat and coach in the back of the plane.” 
It does not bother him at all. He is a big guy. He says, “Mohnish, I was 
fishing in Costa Rica, and at the end of the trip I was going to fly back, 
and I had commercial flight tickets. I had a bad headache. I called 
NetJets, and $80,000 later I was home.” He decided that it would be 
a higher quality of life for him at that point to ignore the commercial 
flight he was going to take and take NetJets straight home because 
he had a headache. I thought that was a prudent use of money by 
him. Not buying the belt was also a prudent use of money. It did not 
make any difference to him. It was interesting to calibrate how he 
thought about expenditures and money.

但这是一段很好的旅程。好消息是，我们身处一个错误率很高的行业。如果你每次下注都投入 10%，一共下 10 次注，那么到最后，你只需要其中一次表现极其出色就够了。这是一个很有利的位置。

Gowzican：
谢谢你，莫尼什。我们的时间快到了。最后一个问题是：我知道，您曾与查理·芒格相处过很多时间。我想知道，您从他那里学到的哪一课，对您的人生影响最大？

莫尼什：
查理和沃伦都是我的朋友。相比沃伦，我和查理要亲近得多，因为我们住在同一个城市。这两个人在公共领域留下的思想和资料都极其丰富，即使从未与他们接触，我们也能从中学到非常多的东西。这很棒。我们不需要与他们建立私人关系。

我从查理那里学到的大部分东西，并不是他亲口对我说的，而是我通过观察他学到的：观察他如何与孩子、孙辈、儿媳、男仆、商业伙伴和朋友相处。我通过观察他如何过每一天的生活来学习。我会去他家，看他如何生活。在这方面，我从查理身上学到了非常多的东西。比如，我注意到，查理腰间的皮带，早在 10 年或 15 年以前就已经磨损得不成样子了，远远超过了使用寿命。这个人可是拥有数十亿美元财富的富豪。他完全可以买一条新皮带，但这对他来说不重要。我去看他时，他穿着一件 Costco 的法兰绒衬衫。这样的衬衫，在 Costco 花 10 美元就能买到。我曾问过他这件事。他很喜欢那些衬衫。我看到的是一个极其富有、却看不出有任何理由轻率挥霍财富的人。

巴菲特说，他们最终说服查理购买了 NetJets 的一份私人飞机共享产权。巴菲特说，要说服查理购买 NetJets 来乘坐私人飞机，是一场很难做成的推销。我跟查理聊过这件事。我说：“查理，你曾跟我说，你多么喜欢乘坐西南航空，坐在飞机后部经济舱的中间座位。”这对他完全不是问题。他是个大块头。他说：“莫尼什，我当时在哥斯达黎加钓鱼。行程结束后准备飞回去，已经买好了民航机票。可我头痛得厉害。我打电话给 NetJets，花了 8 万美元后，我就到家了。”他认为，在那个时候，放弃原本要搭乘的民航航班，坐 NetJets 直接回家，会让自己的生活质量更高，因为他头痛。我认为，他这样花钱很明智。不买新皮带，同样是明智地使用金钱。换不换皮带，对他没有任何影响。细细体会他如何看待开支和金钱，是件很有意思的事。

仅依据实际上传 PDF 及该 PDF 的提取文本；未使用网页版本。

结构与完整性
- 共 14 页，page 值 1 至 14 连续，完整保留原始分页。
- 共 78 个段落，与源文按空行划分的 78 个段落逐页一一对应。
- 发言人通常与紧随其后的正文位于同一个 paragraphs 字符串，二者之间保留换行。第 10、11、14 页原文单列的 Gowzican 标签保留为单独段落。
- 第 2/3、3/4、4/5、6/7、10/11、11/12 页之间的承接均保留；尤其第 10/11 页跨页的 30 亿美元数值按原页放置。
- 第 1 页完整题名、日期和免责声明已译；第 14 页重复的完整免责声明再次保留，两个声明字符串完全一致。
- 全部主持人/提问者发言及莫尼什的回答保留，未做摘要或省略重复。
- 专名莫尼什、帕伯莱、巴菲特、芒格及复利统一。Gowzican、Reysas、Kaspi、Johnny、Anthony、Miguel、Jakob Wilkin、Will Hansen 等按原文保留。
- 已人工逐段复核语义和金额、年份、百分比；金额以中文万/亿单位准确换算。

源文疑点及处理
1. 第 4 页：源文把 1972—2026 年间沃尔玛和标普 500 的年化收益都写为约 15% 或 16%，又称只剩初始占比 2% 的沃尔玛的组合每年领先标普约 5%。这些数字明显不能同时成立，译文忠实保留，不自行更正。
2. 第 6 页：源文三处在“80 million”人数前加美元符号（$80 million humans / citizens / serve the $80 million）。已在实际 PDF 图像中确认，并非提取错误。译文按人数语境译为“8,000 万人”，人数本身不变；美元符号视为源文笔误，未将人误译成美元。
3. 第 9 页：原文为“34 brothers and sisters”，实际 PDF 图像确认。译文保留“34 个兄弟姐妹”，未擅改成“3 或 4 个”。
4. 第 10 页：主持人说问题来自 Jakob Wilkin，下一位发言人的标记及自我介绍却都是 Johnny。译文完整保留原文这一不一致。
5. 第 11 页：原文“court tailors”在上下文疑为“coattailers”的转录误写；已在 PDF 图像确认。译文写“跟风者”，并在同处明确加〔译注：原文作 court tailors，疑为 coattailers 的转录误写〕，没有把推断伪装成原文事实。
6. 第 11 页：原文“hub business”含义不明，已在 PDF 图像确认。译文保留为“hub 业务”，未擅自改成核心业务或整体业务。
7. 原文第 4 页关于沃尔顿家族从不卖股、若干股票归零，第 6 页里拉跌幅等陈述均按原文翻译，没有使用外部事实去修改说话者的论断。
